# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“Indeed, two weeks back, the eighth infant was born,” Miss Winifred remarked, seated in a rocking chair in front of the hearth inside the tiny dwelling on a crisp afternoon in October. “A girl was born. Gideon lost his temper completely—claiming a boy was what he desired—though actually he had no wish for the child whatsoever. Had a boy arrived, he would have raged over it not being a girl. Their previous children consisted of four girls and three boys, which makes me think the gender of this newborn hardly mattered, yet naturally he was compelled to be disagreeable, as men always are. Outfitted in its lovely small garments, the infant is truly attractive. Dark eyes belong to it, along with the most charming, minuscule hands.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0000 }

“I have to go look at it, as I simply adore infants,” Nell remarked, grinning inwardly at an idea far too precious and holy to express aloud.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0001 }

“They are nice, I cannot deny,” Miss Winifred conceded. “However, take my word for it, certain people appear to possess a surplus beyond necessity. Eleven were born to my unfortunate cousin Flora up at the Glen, making her an absolute drudge! It was three years ago that her husband took his own life. Precisely what a man would do!”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0002 }

“Why did he act in such a manner?” Nell inquired, feeling somewhat taken aback.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0003 }

“He failed to have his own way about some matter, which led him to leap down the well. We are well rid of him! From birth, he was a bully. Naturally, the well was ruined by this. Poor Flora simply could not stand the idea of relying on it ever again! Consequently, she paid to have a new one constructed, incurring a terrible cost for water that turned out to be extremely hard. Had he been determined to drown, surely the harbor offered an abundance of water? A person of that sort exhausts my patience. During my time here, Seven Gulls has experienced merely two suicides. Frank Ainslie—who was Lorna Vane’s father—was the second one. On a side note, has Lorna come by to visit you yet?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0004 }

“No, but I bumped into her on the beach a couple of evenings back and we struck up a conversation,” said Nell, suddenly listening intently.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0005 }

Miss Winifred gave a nod.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0006 }

“I am happy, dearie. I had been hoping you would get together with her. How do you feel about her?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0007 }

“She seemed extremely attractive to me.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0008 }

“Oh, certainly. No person around Seven Gulls was ever capable of matching her beauty. Have you ever viewed her hair? It extends all the way down to her feet whenever she unbinds it. However, my question was how did she appeal to you?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0009 }

“I feel that I might become quite fond of her should she allow it,” Nell stated unhurriedly.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0010 }

“Yet she refused to allow you—she shoved you away and maintained her distance from you. Unfortunate Lorna! Knowing the nature of her past existence would leave you hardly astonished. That existence has been a tragedy—a tragedy!” Miss Winifred forcefully reiterated.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0011 }

“I would be glad if you could relate her whole story to me, provided you are able to do so while keeping any confidences intact.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0012 }

“Goodness, dear, all the folks in Seven Gulls are aware of poor Lorna’s tale. The EXTERNAL details aren't a secret at all. Only Lorna knows the INTERNAL truth, and she refuses to share her private thoughts with anyone. I suppose I’m pretty much the closest companion she possesses in the world, yet she has not spoken a single grievance to me. Have you ever laid eyes on Rufus Vane?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0013 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0014 }

“Well, I might just as well start from the very start and relate the entire story to you sequentially, which will enable you to comprehend it. As I stated previously, Frank Ainslie was Lorna’s father. He possessed intelligence and lacked ambition—in typical male fashion. Oh, he was blessed with an abundance of intellect—and a lot of benefit he derived from it! He commenced attending college, remaining there for a period of two years, after which his well-being collapsed. A tendency toward consumption existed throughout the Ainslie family. Consequently, Frank returned to his family home and initiated a farming career. He took as his wife Rose Kerr, who hailed from across the harbor. Rose held the reputation of being the most beautiful person in Seven Gulls—Lorna inherits her appearance from her mother, yet she possesses tenfold the energy and drive that Rose displayed, along with a vastly superior physique. Now, Nell, as you are aware, my position is consistently that we female folk should support one another. Heaven knows we are subjected to a sufficient amount of hardship from men, which is why I maintain that we should refrain from attacking each other, and rarely will you catch me disparaging a fellow woman. Nevertheless, I possessed little regard for Rose Kerr. To start with, trust ME, she was pampered, and she amounted to nothing more than an indolent, self-centered, complaining individual. Frank lacked any inclination toward labor, resulting in their being as impoverished as Job’s turkey. Impoverished! Trust ME, they subsisted on potatoes and point. A pair of children were born to them—Lorna and Julian. Lorna possessed the physical appearance of her mother alongside the intellect of her father, plus a quality inherited from neither parent. She inherited the traits of her Grandmother West—a magnificent elderly woman. During her childhood, Nell, she was the most intelligent, warm, and cheerful creature. All people held affection for her. She stood as the preferred child of her father, and she held immense affection for him in return. The two of them were 'chums,’ to use her own term. She proved incapable of perceiving any of his defects—and he TRULY was an appealing kind of man in particular respects.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0015 }

“Well, Lorna was twelve years old when the initial terrible event occurred. Little Julian was four years younger than her, and she adored him—and he TRULY was a sweet little fellow. Then he was killed one day—he fell from a large load of hay precisely as it entered the barn, and the wheel rolled directly over his tiny body, crushing his life out. And remember, Nell, Lorna witnessed it. Her eyes were on him from the loft. A single screech escaped her—the hired man claimed no sound in all his life had ever equaled it—he declared it would echo in his ears until driven out by Gabriel’s trump. Yet she never uttered another screech or wept over it afterward. From the loft she leaped onto the load and then from the load down to the floor, where she snatched up the little bleeding, warm, lifeless body, Nell—they were forced to tear it away from her before she’d release it. They summoned me—I cannot speak about it.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0016 }

Drying the tears from her gentle brown eyes, Miss Winifred worked her needle in painful quiet for a little while.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0017 }

“Well,” she continued, “everything had ended—little Julian was laid to rest in the cemetery above the harbor, and when some time had passed, Lorna returned to her studies and her school. Julian’s name was never spoken by her—from then until now, I have not heard it pass her lips. I suppose that ancient pain continues to ache and burn occasionally; nevertheless she was merely a child, and time treats children very gently, Nell, dearie. Eventually her laughter returned—her laugh was the sweetest thing. It is rarely heard these days.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0018 }

“I listened to it one evening recently,” stated Nell. “It REALLY IS a lovely laugh.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0019 }

“Following the passing of Julian, Frank Ainslie started a downward slide. Being frail, he suffered a heavy blow from it, since he truly adored the youth, even if, as I mentioned earlier, Lorna remained his preferred one. Becoming gloomy and despondent, he either lacked the ability or the desire to labor. Then, on a certain day when Lorna reached fourteen, he took his own life by hanging—specifically in the parlor, no less, Nell, directly in the center of the parlor suspended from the lamp hook attached to the ceiling. Was that not typical of a man? Furthermore, it coincided with his wedding anniversary. A pleasant, tasteful moment to select for such a deed, wouldn't you say? Naturally, that unfortunate Lorna ended up being the person who discovered him. She walked into the parlor during that morning, singing while carrying some new blooms for the vases, and at that spot she caught sight of her father suspended from the ceiling, possessing a face that was as black as coal. Believe ME, it was a terrible thing!”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0020 }

“Oh, how awful!” Nell exclaimed, shivering. “That poor, unfortunate child!”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0021 }

“Lorna refrained from weeping at the funeral of her father, just as she had not wept at Julian’s. Rose, on the other hand, shrieked and wailed enough for both of them, leaving Lorna fully occupied as she attempted to soothe and console her mother. Rose filled me with disgust, a feeling shared by all the others, yet Lorna never lost her composure. Her mother was someone she loved. Lorna possesses a loyal nature—in her view, her relatives were incapable of fault. Anyway, Frank Ainslie was laid to rest next to Julian, and a massive monument was erected for him by Rose. Take MY word for it, it exceeded the size of his character! At any rate, its cost surpassed what Rose was able to pay, given that the mortgage on the farm exceeded what the property was worth. Shortly afterward, however, Lorna’s elderly grandmother West passed away, leaving Lorna a modest sum of money—an amount sufficient to fund one year for her at Regent’s Academy. Lorna was determined to qualify as a teacher if possible, and subsequently earn the funds needed to put herself through Wexcombe College. Her father had cherished that very plan—he desired that she obtain what he had forfeited. Lorna overflowed with ambition, and her mind was packed with intelligence. She attended Regent’s, where she completed two years of studies in a single year to earn her First; upon returning home, she secured the position at the Glen school. She was filled with such joy, hope, vitality, and enthusiasm. Reflecting on her nature during those days compared to her present state makes me say—drat the men!”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0022 }

Miss Winifred cut her thread away with a hostility that suggested she was slicing through the throat of humanity in a single blow, as if she were Nero.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0023 }

“Rufus Vane entered her life during that summer. His father, Abner Vane, managed a store at the Glen, yet Rufus inherited a nautical inclination from his mother; he was accustomed to sailing during the summer and working as a clerk in his father's store throughout the winter. He was a large, good-looking man, possessing a small, wicked soul. He continuously desired a thing until he obtained it, whereupon he ceased to desire it—precisely as a man does. Oh, he refrained from complaining about the weather whenever it was pleasant, and he was usually quite pleasant and amiable whenever all went well. However, he consumed a great deal of alcohol, and several unpleasant tales were recounted regarding him and a young woman down at the fishing village. He was not suitable for Lorna to wipe her feet upon, to put it plainly. Furthermore, he was a Methodist! Yet he was utterly crazy about her—due to her attractive appearance initially, and due to her refusal to speak to him subsequently. He swore he would possess her—and he obtained her!”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0024 }

“In what manner did he manage to accomplish this?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0025 }

“Oh, that was a truly wicked deed! Rose Ainslie will never have my forgiveness. You see, dearie, the mortgage on the farm belonging to the Ainslies was held by Abner Vane, with the interest remaining unpaid for a number of years, so Rufus went right to Mrs. Ainslie and declared that unless Lorna became his wife, he would persuade his father to foreclose on the property. Rose acted dreadfully—she swooned, cried, and begged Lorna to prevent her from being cast out of her dwelling. She claimed her heart would shatter if she had to depart from the place she had entered as a bride. I would not have held it against her for feeling terribly grieved about it—yet you would not have expected her to be self-centered enough to offer up her own kin on account of it, would you? Well, that is precisely what she was.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0026 }

“And Lorna yielded—her love for her mother was so great that she would have performed any deed to spare her agony. She wedded Rufus Vane. At that moment, not one of us understood the reason. Only much later did I discover how her mother had nagged her into the match. Still, I was convinced that something was amiss, since I was aware of how repeatedly she had rejected him, and such a sudden reversal was out of character for Lorna. Furthermore, I was certain that Rufus Vane was not the sort of man Lorna could ever care for, regardless of his handsome appearance and lively manners. Naturally, there was no grand wedding, yet Rose requested that I attend their marriage. I attended, but I regretted going. I had observed Lorna’s expression during the funeral of her brother and during the funeral of her father—and at that moment, it felt to me as though I were witnessing it at her own funeral. Yet Rose was beaming like a basket of chips, believe ME!
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0027 }

“Lorna and Rufus established themselves on the Ainslie place—Rose was unable to endure being separated from her dear daughter!—and resided there during the winter. When spring arrived, Rose caught pneumonia and passed away—a year later than she should have! Lorna experienced quite a bit of heartbreak because of it. Isn’t it awful how certain unworthy people are cherished, whereas others who are much more deserving, one would imagine, never receive much love? Regarding Rufus, he had grown tired of peaceful domestic existence—exactly like a man. He wanted to pack up and leave. He traveled over to Nova Scotia so he could see his relatives—his father originated from Nova Scotia—and he sent a letter back to Lorna stating that Laurence Vane, his cousin, was embarking on a sea trip to Havana and he planned to go along. The ship's name was the Four Sisters and their absence was expected to last roughly nine weeks.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0028 }

“Lorna must have felt a sense of relief. However, she kept silent. Starting from her wedding day, her demeanor matched her current one—aloof and haughty, maintaining a wall between herself and all people save for me. Mark MY words, I refuse to BE pushed away! Despite all circumstances, I have simply held onto Lorna as tightly as I possibly could.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0029 }

“According to her, you were her closest friend,” Nell stated.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0030 }

“Was that what she did?” Miss Winifred cried out with great joy. “I am truly grateful to know that. There were times I questioned whether my presence was truly desired by her, given that she never allowed me to believe it was. Your effect in warming her up must have exceeded your expectations, or she would not have uttered even that much to you. Ah, what a miserable, sorrow-stricken girl! Whenever Rufus Vane comes into my sight, I am filled with a desire to plunge a knife right through his body.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0031 }

Miss Winifred dabbed her eyes a second time, and after easing her emotions with that violent desire, resumed her narrative.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0032 }

“Well, Lorna remained over on that side by herself. Before his departure, Rufus had sown the crop, and it was tended by old Abner. As the summer passed, the Four Sisters failed to return. An inquiry was made by the Nova Scotia Vanes, who discovered that the vessel had reached Havana, unloaded her freight, laden a new one, and departed bound for home; beyond that point, their discoveries ended completely. As time went on, folks started speaking of Rufus Vane as a deceased man. Nearly everybody was convinced of his death, even if nobody was sure, since sailors have reappeared here at the harbor following absences of many years. Lorna was certain he had not died—and her belief was correct. A terrible shame, as well! During the following summer, Captain Saul happened to be in Havana—which occurred prior to his retirement from nautical life, naturally. He decided to investigate a little—Captain Saul was forever interfering, as men so often are—and he began making inquiries in sailors’ boarding houses and similar establishments, attempting to learn any details regarding the crew belonging to the Four Sisters. It would have served him better to leave well enough alone, to my mind! Anyway, he visited a certain remote location, and there he discovered a person who he recognized immediately as Rufus Vane, despite the large beard he wore. Captain Saul had him shaved, leaving zero uncertainty—it was indeed Rufus Vane—physically, at any rate. His intellect was gone—and as far as a soul goes, I don't believe he ever possessed one!”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0033 }

“What had occurred with him?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0034 }

“No one understands the exact truth about it. The boarding house owners could only state that roughly twelve months prior, they had discovered him slumped on their front steps one morning in a terrible state—with his head beaten nearly to a pulp. Their assumption was that he had been injured during a drunken brawl, which is probably accurate. They brought him inside, believing there was no chance he would survive. Yet he survived—and upon recovering, he was exactly like a child. He lacked memory, intellect, or the capacity to reason. Attempts were made to discover his identity, but they always failed. He was unable to state his own name—he could merely speak a handful of basic words. A letter was in his possession that started 'Dear Rufus’ and ended with 'Lorna,’ yet it lacked an address and had lost its envelope. They permitted him to remain—he was taught to perform some simple chores around the property—and that is where Captain Saul discovered him. He brought him back—a deed I have constantly called a unfortunate day's labor, even if I suppose no alternative existed for him. His hope was that upon returning home and viewing his previous environment and known faces, Rufus would regain his memory. However, it produced no result. He has remained at the residence up the brook from that time onward. He is simply like a child, neither more nor less. He exhibits bad-tempered periods at times, but he is usually merely blank, pleasant, and inoffensive. He tends to wander off if he is left unwatched. That represents the load Lorna has been forced to bear for eleven years—and entirely by herself. Old Abner Vane passed away shortly after the return of Rufus, whereupon it was discovered that he was nearly broke. Following the settlement of affairs, Lorna and Rufus were left with only the old Ainslie farm. Lorna leased it to John Ward, and that rental payment comprises her entire income. On occasion during the summer, she accommodates a lodger to assist her finances. Nevertheless, the majority of tourists favor the opposite shore of the harbor containing the hotels and vacation cottages. Lorna’s residence sits at too great a distance from the swimming beach. She has provided care for Rufus without leaving his side for eleven years—she is bound to that simpleton forever. And this follows every dream and expectation she formerly possessed! It is easy to envision her existence, Nell, dearie—given her attractiveness, animation, self-respect, and intelligence. It has been nothing short of a living death.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0035 }

“Poor, poor girl!” Nell repeated. She felt chided by her personal joy. When another individual was bound to be that wretched, what entitlement did she possess to experience such happiness?
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0036 }

“Would you explain to me precisely what Lorna stated and the way she behaved the evening you encountered her by the water?” Miss Winifred inquired.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0037 }

Giving her full attention, she listened and indicated her approval with a nod.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0038 }

“YOU believed she was formal and unemotional, Nell, my sweet, yet I am able to assure you that she warmed up remarkably for someone like her. She surely took a genuine liking to you. I am delighted. You might prove very helpful to her. It was a relief to learn that a newly married pair was moving into this dwelling, as I trusted it would bring Lorna some companionship; particularly if you were part of the group that understands Joseph. You WILL become her friend, won’t you, Nell, my sweet?”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0039 }

“Indeed I will, if she’ll let me,” Nell said, showing all of her characteristic, sweet, and impulsive earnestness.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0040 }

“Regardless of whether she allows it, your duty is to be her friend,” Miss Winifred stated with determination. “If she acts aloof occasionally, ignore it—do not pay it any attention. Consider what her existence used to be—and currently is—and inevitably will remain, I assume, because individuals such as Rufus Vane never die, as far as I know. You ought to observe the weight he has gained following his return home. Formerly, he was quite thin. Simply FORCE her to accept your friendship—you possess the capability—you belong to the sort of people with that talent. However, you cannot afford to be easily offended. Furthermore, do not care if she appears reluctant to have you visit her house often. She understands that certain women dislike being in the presence of Rufus—they protest that he makes their skin crawl. Merely persuade her to visit this place as frequently as possible. Her opportunities to leave are limited—she is unable to abandon Rufus for extended periods, since Heaven only knows what he might perform—he would probably set the residence on fire. Her freedom occurs almost exclusively during nighttime, once he has retired to bed and drifted off to sleep. He consistently turns in at an early hour and rests deeply until the following day. That probably explains why you encountered her by the water. She frequently roams around that area.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0041 }

“I will do everything I can for her,” said Nell. The fascination she felt for Lorna Vane, which had been lively from the moment she observed her herding her geese down the slope, grew a thousand times stronger because of Miss Winifred’s story. Her heart was drawn by an overpowering attraction to the girl’s attractiveness, grief, and solitude. Never before had she met someone of her kind; until now, her companions had been healthy, ordinary, cheerful girls resembling herself, whose youthfulness was darkened merely by ordinary human troubles and losses. Lorna Vane existed separately, an unhappy, moving embodiment of obstructed womanhood. Nell made up her mind to gain access to the realm of that isolated spirit and discover the fellowship it was so capable of bestowing, if not for the harsh bonds confining it within a dungeon not constructed by itself.
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0042 }

“And remember this, Nell, dearie,” Miss Winifred remarked, having not yet entirely unburdened her mind, “You ought not to suppose Lorna is an unbeliever since she scarcely ever attends church—or even that she belongs to the Methodists. Naturally, she cannot bring Rufus to church—not that he attended church very often during his finest days. But simply keep in mind that she remains a truly devoted Presbyterian in her soul, Nell, dearie.”
{: #nw-v04-c11-p0043 }
